doc.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 16, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Education as the most important project
summary: Of his many projects Powell puts education first, as a jazz activist, and ties it to his New Orleans family's belief in schooling.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: You told me you had about 40 projects on the burner and, we’ll get to maybe the first five anyway, but—

Well I guess the first one that’s the most important to me is education. I consider myself a jazz activist, therefore I can be active from kindergarten to Congress. Because of my studying acting or performing, I can perform in front of Congress just as well as I can perform in front of a kindergarten class. So I do consider myself — now education is the most important. It’s through the education that I had that allows me all this freedom to wear whatever I want to. And to my family, education is most important. I’ll give you a good example. I wish I had brought the pictures. Christmas I spent time with the youngest musician in my family. Musicians. They are two sisters. They played at Constitution Hall and Kennedy Center already, and their ages are three and five. They’re studying the Suzuki method. My family has all sort of beautiful educational things. In my sister’s home in Washington, D.C., she has on the kitchen table a book of gratitudes. And when anything — anybody comes in the house — they say, “Wow, I’m grateful I got home, I had a—” she’ll write it down. So actually, and it’s beautiful and it’s one of the most intelligent things I ever heard of. But education is important to my family. We come from New Orleans and I guess we were told in my era, a lot of things we couldn’t do. And we knew then that education was the key to it. But I think for most people from the

south, they have a keener desire, or they can see the feasibility of being educated. Because I know when I used to travel in Texas and Kentucky and all of that, the southern people have another thing about education. In fact, most of the black colleges are in the south. But anyway, in my family, because of education, it’s always been important to me. I know it’s allowed me the life that I have now. But you can see how early it can start. And if it starts at that age, well there’s no big deal about it. You just know if you want to learn something, you have to work at it.
You’ve been able to take your practical experience as a player and channel it into an educational delivery to the public schools?
